description: The pathway of air, breathing mechanics and how gas exchange in the alveoli supports activity.
content_html:
Breathing and Gas Exchange

Every sporting action requires energy, and most energy for sustained activity comes from aerobic respiration, which demands a continuous supply of oxygen and an efficient means of removing carbon dioxide. The respiratory system provides both. It moves air in and out of the body, extracts oxygen from inhaled air and expels the CO&sub2; produced by working muscles. Understanding the pathway of air, the mechanics of breathing and the process of gas exchange at the alveoli underpins everything else in applied anatomy and physiology.

The Pathway of Air

Air enters through the nose or mouth and travels down the trachea (windpipe) into the chest. The trachea divides into two bronchi (singular: bronchus), one entering each lung. Inside the lungs, each bronchus branches repeatedly into smaller and smaller airways called bronchioles. At the end of each bronchiole sits a cluster of tiny air sacs called alveoli (singular: alveolus). It is here, at the alveoli, that oxygen passes into the bloodstream and carbon dioxide passes out.

The diaphragm is the primary muscle of breathing. It sits below the lungs as a dome-shaped sheet of muscle. The external intercostal muscles run between the ribs and assist breathing by raising the ribcage. Together, these structures create the pressure changes that move air in and out.

Breathing Mechanics

During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens downward, while the external intercostal muscles contract and lift the ribcage upward and outward. This increases the volume of the thoracic (chest) cavity, reducing the air pressure inside. Air rushes in down the pressure gradient from the higher-pressure atmosphere into the lower-pressure lungs.

During exhalation at rest, the diaphragm and external intercostals relax. The elastic recoil of the lung tissue and the weight of the ribcage cause the thoracic volume to decrease, pressure rises above atmospheric, and air is pushed out. During exercise, when faster and deeper breathing is needed, the internal intercostal muscles and abdominal muscles actively assist exhalation by compressing the thoracic cavity further.

Tidal Volume and Vital Capacity

Tidal volume is the amount of air moved per breath. At rest, a typical adult’s tidal volume is about 0.5 litres. During maximal exercise, tidal volume can rise to around 3 litres as the body demands more oxygen. This increase is due to the deeper contractions of the diaphragm and the active engagement of the intercostal and abdominal muscles.

Vital capacity is the maximum amount of air that can be exhaled after a maximal inhalation. It is used as a measure of lung capacity and typically ranges from 3 to 6 litres depending on body size, sex and training status. Endurance athletes tend to have higher vital capacities than untrained individuals, partly due to strengthening of the respiratory muscles and increased chest wall flexibility. Regular aerobic training can modestly increase vital capacity over time.

Key Fact

Air pathway: nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi (one per lung) → bronchioles → alveoli. At the alveoli: O&sub2; diffuses into blood; CO&sub2; diffuses out. Tidal volume rises from ~0.5 L at rest to ~3 L during maximal exercise. Vital capacity is the maximum air exhaled after a full breath in.

Gas Exchange at the Alveoli

Gas exchange works by diffusion — gases move from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration across a thin membrane. The alveoli are designed to maximise the rate of diffusion. Each alveolus is surrounded by a dense network of pulmonary capillaries. The combined wall of the alveolus and the capillary is only two cells thick, providing the shortest possible diffusion distance.

Inhaled air is richer in oxygen (about 21%) than the deoxygenated blood arriving from the working muscles (which has used most of its oxygen). Oxygen therefore diffuses from the alveolar air into the blood. Carbon dioxide concentration is higher in the blood (produced by aerobic respiration in the muscles) than in the alveolar air, so CO&sub2; diffuses from the blood into the alveolus to be exhaled. This simultaneous exchange happens continuously — as long as you are breathing and your heart is beating.

Inhaled air contains approximately 21% oxygen and 0.04% CO&sub2;. Exhaled air contains approximately 16% oxygen and 4% CO&sub2;, reflecting the oxygen taken up and the CO&sub2; expelled. The nitrogen content (~78%) is virtually unchanged because the body neither uses nor produces it.

Key Fact

Inhaled vs exhaled air: O&sub2; falls from ~21% to ~16%; CO&sub2; rises from ~0.04% to ~4%. This difference reflects the oxygen absorbed and CO&sub2; produced by working tissues. At the alveoli, diffusion is maximised by: large surface area, thin membrane, rich blood supply and steep concentration gradients maintained by breathing and circulation.

The respiratory and cardiovascular systems must operate in synchrony. Oxygen absorbed at the alveoli immediately enters the pulmonary capillaries and is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells via the pulmonary vein to the left side of the heart. From there, the left ventricle pumps it out through the aorta to the working muscles. At the muscle capillaries, oxygen diffuses from the blood into the muscle fibres while CO&sub2; diffuses from the fibres into the blood. The blood, now deoxygenated and CO&sub2;-rich, returns via the vena cava to the right side of the heart, is pumped to the lungs, and the cycle repeats. During intense exercise, both systems up-regulate together: breathing rate and depth increase to bring more O&sub2; to the alveoli; heart rate and stroke volume increase to transport it faster. If either system is limited (e.g. by asthma reducing airflow, or anaemia reducing haemoglobin), exercise capacity is compromised.

During maximal, short-duration anaerobic exercise (e.g. a 100 m sprint), the demand for oxygen exceeds what the cardiovascular and respiratory systems can deliver. Muscles shift to anaerobic respiration and accumulate lactic acid. The lungs are still exchanging gases as fast as possible, but the limiting factor is the delivery rate, not the exchange mechanism itself. After the sprint, breathing rate remains elevated to repay the oxygen debt (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, EPOC) — the extra oxygen needed to remove lactic acid and restore the body’s pre-exercise state.
exam_tip_html: When explaining gas exchange, use the word ‘diffusion’ and state the direction of movement for each gas (O&sub2; into blood, CO&sub2; out of blood) with the reason (concentration gradient). Merely writing ‘oxygen goes into the blood and CO&sub2; comes out’ without the mechanism scores only partial credit. On 2-mark Describe questions about breathing, distinguish between the action of the diaphragm (contracts and flattens during inhalation) and the intercostals (lift the ribcage) — naming one but not the other loses a mark. For tidal volume and vital capacity questions, use precise units (litres, L) in your answer.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Air travels: nose/mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. At the alveoli, O&sub2; diffuses into the blood and CO&sub2; diffuses out, driven by concentration gradients.
  • Inhalation: diaphragm contracts (flattens), external intercostals raise the ribcage, thoracic volume increases, pressure drops, air rushes in. Tidal volume rises from ~0.5 L at rest to ~3 L during maximal exercise.
  • Inhaled air is ~21% O&sub2; / ~0.04% CO&sub2;; exhaled air is ~16% O&sub2; / ~4% CO&sub2;. The respiratory and cardiovascular systems work together to deliver O&sub2; to muscles and remove CO&sub2;.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the role of the alveoli?
A) They are the main airways conducting air into the lungs
B) They are the sites of gas exchange between air and blood
C) They are the muscles that inflate the lungs during breathing
D) They store inhaled air before it reaches the bronchioles
practice_questions.marks: B) They are the sites of gas exchange between air and blood [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the approximate percentage of oxygen in inhaled air and in exhaled air.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for inhaled: approximately 21% oxygen. 1 mark for exhaled: approximately 16% oxygen. Accept values within ±1% of these figures.

practice_questions.text: Describe the mechanics of inhalation, naming the muscles involved and explaining why air enters the lungs.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for diaphragm: contracts and flattens, increasing the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity. 1 mark for external intercostals: contract and lift the ribcage upward and outward, increasing the lateral dimension. 1 mark for pressure explanation: increased thoracic volume reduces air pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure, so air moves in from outside down the pressure gradient.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows tidal volume and breathing rate data for a club cyclist at rest and during three stages of a training session.

Stage            | Tidal volume (L) | Breathing rate (breaths/min)
Rest             | 0.5              | 14
Warm-up          | 1.2              | 20
Moderate effort  | 2.1              | 28
Maximal effort   | 2.9              | 38

Calculate the total volume of air breathed per minute (minute ventilation) at rest and at maximal effort.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for rest: 0.5 × 14 = 7.0 L/min. 1 mark for maximal: 2.9 × 38 = 110.2 L/min. Accept correct arithmetic based on the figures given. Units (L/min) required.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the alveoli are well-adapted for efficient gas exchange during high-intensity exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for large surface area: millions of alveoli create a very large total surface area for diffusion. 1 mark for thin membrane: the combined alveolar and capillary wall is only two cells thick, minimising diffusion distance. 1 mark for rich blood supply: dense network of pulmonary capillaries maintains a steep concentration gradient by constantly removing O2 and delivering CO2.

practice_questions.text: A personal trainer is advising a client who has recently completed a course of respiratory physiotherapy following a lung infection. The client is now returning to exercise. Assess the extent to which the respiratory system limits exercise performance compared to the cardiovascular system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Accurately describes the role of the respiratory system (tidal volume, gas exchange, breathing mechanics) and the cardiovascular system (cardiac output, oxygen transport, vascular shunting). Makes a comparative argument: in healthy individuals, the cardiovascular system is usually the primary limiting factor at maximal intensity because cardiac output determines O2 delivery; the respiratory system has surplus capacity. However, in a person recovering from lung infection, reduced alveolar surface area, reduced vital capacity or obstructed airways could make the respiratory system the limiting factor. Reaches a supported, nuanced judgement. Consistent sporting/clinical application.
Secure (3-4): Identifies roles of both systems with mostly correct physiology. Some comparison. Partial judgement.
Developing (2): Describes one system adequately; the other is limited or missing.
Emerging (1): Basic mention of breathing or heart with no comparative analysis.

The volume of air in one breath during normal breathing

knowledge_checks.q: Which direction does oxygen diffuse during gas exchange at the alveoli?
options: From the alveolus into the blood
From the muscle into the blood
From the trachea into the bronchi

knowledge_checks.q: During inhalation, the _____ contracts and flattens, increasing thoracic volume.
The air sacs at the end of the bronchioles where gas exchange occurs are called _____.
Match each component to its role in the respiratory system:
right: Main airway conducting air into the chest
Small airways leading to the alveoli

flashcard_questions.q: What is the correct order of the air pathway into the lungs?
What is tidal volume at rest for a typical adult?
How does tidal volume change during maximal exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Rises to approximately 3 litres per breath.
Maximum air exhaled after a maximal inhalation.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the approximate percentage of oxygen in inhaled air?
What is the approximate percentage of oxygen in exhaled air?
By what process does oxygen cross from alveolus into blood?
flashcard_questions.a: Diffusion — from high to low concentration.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the alveolar-capillary membrane thin?
flashcard_questions.a: To minimise diffusion distance, speeding up gas exchange.

flashcard_questions.q: What muscle is the primary driver of inhalation?
flashcard_questions.a: Diaphragm — contracts and flattens to increase thoracic volume.

flashcard_questions.q: What is lactic acid, and when does it accumulate?
flashcard_questions.a: A by-product of anaerobic respiration that builds up during high-intensity exercise.

glossary_terms.definition: The two main airways branching from the trachea into the left and right lungs.
The smallest airways in the lungs, which lead to the clusters of alveoli where gas exchange takes place.
Tiny air sacs at the end of the bronchioles where gas exchange between air and blood takes place.
The dome-shaped sheet of muscle below the lungs that is the primary muscle of breathing, contracting and flattening to increase thoracic volume during inhalation.
The volume of air inhaled or exhaled in a single breath during normal breathing at rest or during exercise.
The maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximum inhalation, indicating the usable capacity of the lungs.
A by-product of anaerobic respiration that accumulates in muscles, contributing to fatigue and the burning sensation felt during high-intensity exercise.
